title: How to Build Family Traditions That Form Faith
excerpt: Children are formed less by what you say once than by what you do every year. A tradition is a sermon you preach with your hands, repeated until it becomes their bones.
body:
Ask grown adults what shaped their faith, and they rarely cite a sermon or a lesson. They cite a smell, a song, a thing the family always did. The candle that was always lit, the meal that was always eaten, the words that were always said. We are formed less by argument than by repetition, less by what we are told once than by what we do a hundred times. This is not a weakness in human beings. It is how God made us, and a wise parent builds with it instead of against it.

A tradition is a practice repeated until it stops being a decision and becomes part of who the family is. The danger is that traditions form us whether we choose them or not. A family with no intentional rhythms is not a family without traditions; it is a family whose traditions are whatever the culture handed them by default. The choice is not whether to have traditions. It is whether to choose them.

## Why repetition forms more than instruction

The philosopher James K.A. Smith has argued at length that we are not primarily thinking things who occasionally act, but loving things who are shaped by what we do repeatedly. Our loves are trained by liturgies, the rhythms and rituals we practice, whether sacred or commercial. The shopping mall has a liturgy. The stadium has a liturgy. The question for a family is whether its strongest liturgies point toward God or away from him.

Israel understood this in its bones. The whole calendar was built on remembered acts. Passover every spring, the feast of booths every autumn, the Sabbath every week, each one a repeated practice that pressed the story of God into the family until the children could not remember a time they did not know it. "When your children ask you, what does this mean, you shall say." The tradition created the question. The question opened the door to the story.

## Tie traditions to the story of God

A tradition forms faith only if it carries the story. A meal is just a meal until you attach it to something. So build your family's rhythms around the things God has done. A special breakfast on Easter that begins with someone shouting that Christ is risen. A candle lit through Advent. A way you mark baptisms and answered prayers. A blessing spoken every birthday over the child whose year it is.

The particular form matters less than two things: that it repeats, and that it points beyond itself. Choose practices you can actually sustain, because a humble tradition kept for twenty years forms a child more than a grand one abandoned after two.

## Make them sensory

The traditions that stick are the ones a child can taste, hear, touch, and smell. There is a reason God gave Israel a meal and not a memo. A particular food, a particular song, a particular object brought out only on a particular day, these lodge in memory in a way that words alone never do. Years later the smell of that meal will bring the whole meaning back unbidden. Engage the body, and you reach the soul through a door that argument cannot open.

## Keep them simple enough to survive

The enemy of family tradition is grandeur. The parent who plans an elaborate ritual will do it once, exhaust themselves, and quietly let it die. The tradition that survives is the one small enough to keep on a tired year, in a hard season, when money is short and everyone is stretched. Pick practices you can do badly and still do. The forming power is in the repetition, and repetition requires that the thing be light enough to carry for decades.

I have killed good traditions by making them too big. I built something beautiful that demanded too much, did it once, and never again. The children remember the things we did simply and constantly, not the one magnificent attempt that collapsed under its own weight.

## Let the children own them

A tradition becomes a family's own when the children start guarding it. When they say, we always do it this way, when they correct you for getting it wrong, when they insist on it even as teenagers who claim to be too old. That insistence is the tradition working. They are no longer receiving it. They are keeping it. And one day they will carry it into homes of their own, and your grandchildren will think it has always been there.

## This week

Choose one thing God has done, and build one small repeatable practice around it. A blessing at every birthday. A reading and a candle each Sunday of Advent. A particular breakfast on Easter with words that name the resurrection. Make it simple enough to keep on your worst year. Do it once this season, then do it again next time it comes around, and again, until your children cannot remember the family without it.

You are preaching a sermon with your hands. It will outlast every sermon you preach with your mouth.
